overview: Running and building dbt is how you turn your SQL models, tests, seeds, and snapshots into real objects in the warehouse; the CLI commands dbt run, dbt test, and dbt build are the day-to-day verbs that execute your project.

dbt run builds only your models (it materializes CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT), dbt test runs only your data tests against already-built models, and dbt build combines models, tests, seeds, and snapshots into one DAG-ordered command that interleaves each model's tests right after it is built.

Node selection (--select / --exclude), materialization flags like --full-refresh, threading, targets, and run artifacts (run_results.json, manifest.json) give you precise, idempotent, CI-friendly control over exactly what gets built and in what order.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between dbt run, dbt test, and dbt build, and why dbt build is the recommended production command.
Use node selection (--select, --exclude, +, tag:, state:modified+) and flags like --full-refresh and --threads to control what dbt executes.
Read a dbt run summary line (PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP), understand what SKIP means, and use exit codes and run artifacts in CI.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: dbt run, dbt test, and dbt build are subcommands of the dbt CLI that execute a compiled dbt project against a target warehouse. dbt run compiles models and issues their materialization DDL/DML (CREATE VIEW/TABLE AS SELECT, or incremental MERGE) in dependency (DAG) order. dbt test compiles data tests into SELECT queries that must return zero failing rows and executes them against existing relations. dbt build unifies these into a single DAG traversal that runs models, tests, seeds, and snapshots together, executing each resource and its attached tests before proceeding to downstream dependents, so a failing test halts affected downstream nodes. Each invocation is scoped by node-selection flags, writes run artifacts (run_results.json, manifest.json) to the target/ directory, and returns a process exit code for automation.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of your dbt project as a set of recipes (models) and taste-tests (tests). dbt run is the command that actually cooks all the dishes in the right order - it does not taste anything. dbt test is the command that only tastes dishes that are already cooked. dbt build is the smart chef who cooks each dish and immediately tastes it before moving on to any dish that depends on it: if the sauce fails its taste test, the chef refuses to serve the pasta that needed it. Because of that, dbt build stops bad data from flowing downstream mid-run, which is exactly why teams use it in production. The --select flags let you tell the chef 'only make these dishes and everything that depends on them,' so you never have to rebuild the whole menu when you changed one recipe.
coreConcept.historicalContext: In early dbt (pre-2019), the workflow was two separate steps: dbt run to build models, then dbt test to validate them. The problem was ordering - if you ran everything and then tested, bad data could already have propagated into every downstream table before any test ran. dbt 0.18 (2020) introduced dbt build, which interleaves tests with model builds in DAG order so a failing test stops that model's dependents immediately, mirroring how a good CI pipeline fails fast. Around the same era dbt added state-based selection (state:modified+, --defer) to power slim CI, letting teams rebuild only what changed by comparing against a previous run's manifest. These commands and selectors are now the standard vocabulary of every analytics-engineering deployment on Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and Databricks.

whyItMatters.business: Using dbt build means a failed data-quality test stops bad numbers from reaching dashboards mid-run, protecting the trust leadership places in reported metrics like revenue and active users instead of discovering the error after it is on a slide.
whyItMatters.engineering: The distinction between run, test, and build - plus node selection - lets engineers rebuild exactly what changed, run tests in CI, and get deterministic, idempotent, rerun-safe pipelines, drastically cutting debugging time and accidental full rebuilds.
whyItMatters.scalability: Threads parallelize independent DAG branches and state:modified+ selection builds only changed models, so run times stay manageable as a project grows from tens to thousands of models on the same warehouse.
whyItMatters.cost: Selecting a subset of models (state:modified+), avoiding needless --full-refresh, and choosing incremental materializations mean the warehouse recomputes only what is necessary, directly reducing compute spend on every run.
whyItMatters.reliability: build's interleaved testing halts downstream nodes on failure (they show as SKIP), run artifacts and non-zero exit codes drive CI gates, and idempotent materializations make reruns safe - together making pipelines predictable and debuggable.

coreComponents.name: dbt run (build models)
coreComponents.definition: The command that compiles models and executes their materialization DDL/DML (CREATE VIEW/TABLE AS SELECT, or an incremental MERGE) in DAG order; it does NOT run tests.
coreComponents.purpose: To materialize your transformations as physical tables/views in the warehouse.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Resolve ref()/source(), order models by dependency, issue the right SQL per materialization, and write run_results.json.
coreComponents.examples: dbt run | dbt run --select stg_orders+ | dbt run --full-refresh --target prod

coreComponents.name: dbt test (run data tests)
coreComponents.definition: The command that compiles data tests (generic like not_null/unique and singular SQL tests) into SELECT queries expected to return zero rows, run against already-built relations.
coreComponents.purpose: To validate that existing models and sources meet data-quality expectations.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Compile each test to a failing-rows query, execute it, and report PASS/WARN/ERROR based on returned row counts and severity.
coreComponents.examples: dbt test | dbt test --select stg_orders | dbt test --select source:raw

coreComponents.name: dbt build (models + tests + seeds + snapshots)
coreComponents.definition: The recommended production command that runs models, tests, seeds, and snapshots in one DAG traversal, testing each node right after it is built so failures stop downstream dependents.
coreComponents.purpose: To build and validate the whole project fail-fast, so bad data never propagates mid-run.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Traverse the combined DAG, execute each resource and its attached tests, and SKIP downstream nodes when an upstream node errors or a test fails.
coreComponents.examples: dbt build | dbt build --select state:modified+ | dbt build --fail-fast

internalWorking: When you invoke a command, dbt first parses the project and compiles it: it resolves Jinja (ref/source/macros) into a manifest.json describing every node and the DAG of dependencies, and writes fully compiled SQL into the target/compiled directory.

dbt applies your node-selection flags (--select/--exclude and graph operators like model+, +model, tag:, state:modified+) against that DAG to compute the exact set of nodes to execute and prunes the rest.

It then walks the selected DAG in topological order, using the configured number of threads to run independent branches in parallel; for each model it sends the materialization SQL over the adapter to the warehouse, which does the actual compute.

For dbt build specifically, after a model finishes, dbt immediately runs the tests attached to that model before scheduling any downstream node; if the model errors or a test fails, every node that depends on it is not executed and is marked SKIP.

After execution dbt writes run_results.json (per-node status, timing, and the SQL run) to target/, prints the PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP summary, and returns an exit code (0 success, 1 with errors, 2 on usage error) that CI systems use to pass or fail the pipeline.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: dbt CLI invocation (run/test/build) -> parse + compile project (manifest.json, compiled SQL) -> apply node selection (--select/--exclude) -> traverse DAG with N threads -> send SQL to warehouse (models materialize; tests as SELECT COUNT of failing rows) -> build interleaves tests after each node -> failing node SKIPs its dependents -> write run_results.json + print PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP -> exit code to CI
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You run 'dbt build --select stg_orders+' after editing stg_orders; dbt parses the project and builds the manifest and DAG.
2. The selector stg_orders+ resolves to stg_orders plus every model, test, and snapshot downstream of it; unrelated nodes are pruned.
3. dbt executes stg_orders (CREATE VIEW AS SELECT), then immediately runs stg_orders' attached tests (e.g., not_null on order_id) as zero-row SELECTs.
4. Because the tests PASS, dbt proceeds to the downstream mart fct_daily_revenue, builds it as a table, and runs its tests; had a test failed, fct_daily_revenue would be SKIPPED instead.
5. dbt writes run_results.json to target/, prints 'Done. PASS=... WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=...', and returns exit code 0, letting the orchestrator/CI mark the run successful.

keyTerminology.meaning: Flags that pick which resources to run using names, paths, graph operators (model+, +model), and methods (tag:, source:, state:modified+).
keyTerminology.importance: It is how you avoid rebuilding the whole project; targeting only what changed (and its dependents) is essential for fast, cheap runs and slim CI.

keyTerminology.meaning: The four result states in the run summary: PASS = succeeded, WARN = test failed at warn severity, ERROR = model/test failed, SKIP = not executed because an upstream node failed.
keyTerminology.importance: Reading this summary tells you at a glance what broke and, crucially, that SKIP means downstream work was intentionally halted, not silently ignored.

keyTerminology.meaning: A flag that forces incremental models to be dropped and rebuilt from scratch (full CREATE TABLE AS) instead of appending/merging only new rows.
keyTerminology.importance: You need it after changing an incremental model's logic or schema; forgetting it leaves stale or inconsistent data, while overusing it wastes compute.

keyTerminology.meaning: JSON files dbt writes to the target/ directory: manifest.json describes the project graph; run_results.json records each node's status, timing, and SQL from the last invocation.
keyTerminology.importance: They power state comparison (state:modified+), --defer, monitoring, and CI decisions, turning a run into observable, machine-readable output.

importantConcepts.concept: Why dbt build beats separate run then test
importantConcepts.explanation: What: dbt build interleaves each node's tests immediately after it builds, within one DAG traversal, whereas 'dbt run' then 'dbt test' builds every model first and only tests afterward. Why: with run-then-test, if a staging model produces bad data, it has already flowed into every downstream mart before any test runs, so bad numbers reach consumers and you have wasted compute building on garbage. How: build runs stg_orders, tests it, and only if the tests pass does it build the fct model that depends on it; a failure marks dependents SKIP. Pitfall: teams keep the old two-step habit in production and are surprised bad data propagates - use dbt build so failures stop the DAG mid-flight.

What: dbt commands are designed to be safely re-runnable - running the same model again produces the same result. Why: pipelines fail and get retried, and you must be able to rerun without duplicating or corrupting data. How: table/view models use CREATE OR REPLACE (or drop-and-recreate) so a rerun rebuilds the object from its SELECT; incremental models MERGE on a unique key so reruns do not double-insert. Pitfall: writing incremental logic without a proper unique_key or with side effects makes reruns non-idempotent and produces duplicates on retry.

importantConcepts.concept: SKIP is a feature, not an error
importantConcepts.explanation: What: SKIP in the summary means dbt deliberately did not run a node because something it depends on failed. Why: propagating a failure downstream would build tables on top of known-bad data, so dbt stops that branch. How: during a build (or after a model error in run), every dependent of a failed node is marked SKIP and left untouched. Pitfall: reading SKIP as 'something went wrong with that model' - the skipped model is fine; the fix is upstream, at the node that ERRORed or whose test FAILed.

variationsAndTypes: **dbt run:** builds only models (materializes them); no tests. Use during development to quickly rematerialize models.
**dbt test:** runs only data tests against already-built relations; builds nothing. Useful to re-validate without rebuilding.
**dbt build:** models + tests + seeds + snapshots in one DAG-ordered, fail-fast pass - the recommended production command.
**dbt compile / dbt seed / dbt snapshot:** compile generates SQL without executing it; seed loads CSVs into tables; snapshot captures slowly-changing-dimension history.

**Selection & flags:** --select/--exclude with operators (model+, +model, tag:, state:modified+, --defer), plus --full-refresh, --threads, --target dev/prod, and --fail-fast to tune scope, speed, and behavior.
advantages: **Fail-fast data quality:** dbt build interleaves tests so a failure halts downstream nodes, keeping bad data out of consumer tables.
**Precise, cheap runs:** node selection (state:modified+, model+) rebuilds only what changed and its dependents instead of the whole project.
**Idempotent and rerun-safe:** models rebuild deterministically from their SELECTs, so retries after failures do not corrupt or duplicate data.
**CI-friendly automation:** exit codes and run artifacts (run_results.json, manifest.json) let CI gate merges and monitoring track per-node timing and status.
disadvantages: **Command confusion:** beginners expect dbt run to run tests too, or forget --full-refresh on incremental changes, causing silent staleness.
**Whole-warehouse dependency:** every command needs a live warehouse connection and consumes its compute; you cannot build offline.
**Selection complexity:** the graph-operator/selector syntax (+, @, tag:, state:) is powerful but easy to misuse, selecting too much or too little.
**Test coverage gap:** dbt only stops what you actually wrote tests for; unmodeled data-quality issues still slip through build.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use dbt build for scheduled/production runs and CI so models and tests run together fail-fast; use dbt run for quick local iteration on model SQL; use dbt test to re-validate without rebuilding; use state:modified+ in CI to build only changed nodes and --full-refresh when incremental logic or schema changes.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid separate 'dbt run then dbt test' in production (bad data propagates before tests); avoid blanket --full-refresh on every run (wastes compute); avoid running the entire project when a selector would build only the affected subgraph; avoid relying on build to catch problems for which you have written no tests.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Picture an assembly line making a layered cake in stages. dbt run is turning on all the stations and letting every layer get made in order - but nobody checks quality. dbt test is a quality inspector who walks the finished line and checks layers that already exist. dbt build is an inspector standing between every station: as soon as the sponge layer is baked it is checked, and only if it passes does the frosting station receive it; if the sponge fails inspection, every downstream station is halted (SKIP) so you do not waste frosting on a ruined cake. --select is telling the line 'only run the chocolate-cake stations and everything after them,' and --full-refresh is scrapping a half-built layer and remaking it from scratch rather than patching it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: dbt run also runs my tests, so if it succeeds my data is validated.
commonMisconceptions.reality: dbt run only materializes models; it never runs data tests. To validate you must run dbt test, or use dbt build which runs models and their tests together. A green 'dbt run' says nothing about data quality.

commonMisconceptions.myth: dbt build and 'dbt run && dbt test' are equivalent.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They differ in ordering. build interleaves each model's tests right after it builds and SKIPs downstream nodes on failure, stopping bad data mid-DAG. run-then-test builds everything first (so bad data already propagated) and only tests at the end, plus build also handles seeds and snapshots.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A SKIP in the summary means that model failed or has a bug.
commonMisconceptions.reality: SKIP means dbt intentionally did not run the node because an upstream node ERRORed or a test FAILed. The skipped model is not broken; the real problem is upstream. Fix the ERROR/FAIL and the skipped nodes will build on the next run.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Increase --threads so dbt runs independent DAG branches in parallel against the warehouse, size the virtual warehouse to the workload, and use state:modified+ so scheduled/CI runs build only changed nodes; incremental materializations keep large models from full-rebuilding each run.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Run dbt build (not run-then-test) so tests gate each node and failures SKIP dependents; rely on idempotent materializations so retries are safe, and treat a non-zero exit code as a hard failure in the orchestrator.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: On failure, dbt marks dependents SKIP rather than building on bad data; you can rerun from the failure using selectors, and --fail-fast can abort early to save compute when any node errors.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Ingest run_results.json for per-node status and timing and manifest.json for the graph; track PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP counts, run duration, and test failure trends, and alert on non-zero exit codes.
productionConsiderations.security: Warehouse credentials come from profiles.yml/secrets and the --target selects dev vs prod roles; run production builds under a least-privilege service role scoped to the schemas dbt manages, never with a personal or admin account.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoid unnecessary --full-refresh, use incremental models for large append-heavy tables, select only modified nodes (state:modified+) in CI, and schedule builds to match real data freshness rather than running the full project constantly.
productionConsiderations.performance: Tune the warehouse SQL (filter early, avoid needless table materializations), raise threads to parallelize, materialize reused heavy logic as tables, and use --defer with a production manifest to skip rebuilding unchanged upstreams in CI.

codeExamples.title: run vs test vs build: the three core commands
codeExamples.overview: The everyday CLI workflow showing what each command does and the log output that distinguishes them.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Build ONLY models (materialize CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT). No tests run.
dbt run

# 2) Run ONLY data tests against already-built models (SELECTs that must return 0 rows).
dbt test

# 3) Recommended for production: models + tests + seeds + snapshots in DAG order,
#    testing each node right after it builds so failures stop downstream dependents.
dbt build

# Verify the warehouse connection before anything else
dbt debug
codeExamples.breakdown: dbt run materializes models only - a green run does NOT mean your data passed any test. dbt test compiles each test into a query counting failing rows and runs it against existing relations. dbt build unifies models, tests, seeds, and snapshots into one fail-fast DAG traversal, interleaving each model's tests immediately after it is built. dbt debug is the sanity check you run first to confirm credentials and connectivity.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Running with dbt=1.9.0
Registered adapter: snowflake=1.9.0
Found 12 models, 5 tests, 2 seeds, 1 snapshot, 2 sources

Concurrency: 4 threads (target='dev')

1 of 12 OK created sql view model analytics.stg_orders ........ [OK in 0.9s]
2 of 12 OK created sql view model analytics.stg_customers ..... [OK in 0.8s]
...
12 of 12 OK created sql table model analytics.fct_daily_revenue [OK in 1.6s]

Finished running 8 view models, 4 table models in 9.42s.
Completed successfully

Done. PASS=12 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=12
codeExamples.commonIssues: Expecting 'dbt run' to validate data - it does not run tests; use dbt test or dbt build. Running any command without a valid profiles.yml target throws a connection error (diagnose with dbt debug).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use dbt build in scheduled/production jobs so tests run alongside models; keep dbt run for fast local iteration where you do not need tests each time.

codeExamples.title: Node selection, full-refresh, threads, and targets
codeExamples.overview: The flags that control exactly what dbt executes, how fast, and against which environment.
codeExamples.code:
# Build a model and everything downstream of it (the + suffix = descendants)
dbt build --select stg_orders+

# Build a model and everything upstream of it (the + prefix = ancestors)
dbt run --select +fct_daily_revenue

# Select by tag, and exclude a heavy model
dbt build --select tag:finance --exclude fct_huge_events

# Slim CI: build only nodes that changed vs a previous run's manifest, plus their children
dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts

# Rebuild an incremental model FROM SCRATCH (drops + recreates instead of merging new rows)
dbt run --select fct_events --full-refresh

# Run against production with more parallelism, and stop on the first error
dbt build --target prod --threads 8 --fail-fast
codeExamples.breakdown: model+ selects the node and its descendants; +model selects the node and its ancestors. tag: selects by config tag and --exclude prunes nodes. state:modified+ compares the current graph to a stored manifest (--state) and builds only changed nodes and their children - the basis of slim CI; --defer lets unchanged upstreams resolve to the prod objects instead of rebuilding them. --full-refresh forces incremental models to drop and fully rebuild. --threads sets parallelism, --target picks the dev/prod profile, and --fail-fast aborts on the first failure to save compute.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Running with dbt=1.9.0
Found 12 models, 5 tests, 2 sources

Concurrency: 8 threads (target='prod')

1 of 4 START sql view model analytics.stg_orders ............. [RUN]
1 of 4 OK created sql view model analytics.stg_orders ........ [OK in 1.1s]
2 of 4 OK created sql table model analytics.fct_daily_revenue  [OK in 2.3s]
3 of 4 PASS not_null_fct_daily_revenue_order_date ........... [PASS in 0.5s]
4 of 4 PASS unique_fct_daily_revenue_order_date ............. [PASS in 0.6s]

Done. PASS=4 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=4
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting --full-refresh after changing incremental logic leaves stale rows. Confusing model+ (downstream) with +model (upstream). Using state:modified+ without a valid --state manifest path errors out.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: In CI use 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' to build only what changed and defer unchanged upstreams to prod, cutting run time and compute dramatically.

codeExamples.title: A failing test in dbt build: how SKIP protects downstream data
codeExamples.overview: A model whose test fails during build, plus the resulting summary showing an ERROR and a SKIP.
codeExamples.code:
-- models/staging/stg_orders.sql (materialized as a view)
select
    id            as order_id,
    customer_id,
    lower(status) as status,
    amount_cents / 100.0 as order_amount
from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}

# models/staging/_stg.yml  (attach a test that will fail if any status is unexpected)
version: 2
models:
  - name: stg_orders
    columns:
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['completed', 'pending', 'cancelled']

# Command: build stg_orders and its downstream mart together
# (fct_daily_revenue depends on stg_orders via ref('stg_orders'))
dbt build --select stg_orders+
codeExamples.breakdown: dbt build materializes stg_orders, then immediately runs its accepted_values test as a SELECT counting rows whose status is NOT in the allowed list. Because a bad status ('refunded') exists, the test returns 3 failing rows, so it ERRORs. Since fct_daily_revenue depends on stg_orders, dbt refuses to build it and marks it SKIP - preventing bad data from reaching the mart. A plain 'dbt run' would have built both models with no test at all.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
Running with dbt=1.9.0
Found 12 models, 5 tests, 2 sources

1 of 3 OK created sql view model analytics.stg_orders ........ [OK in 0.9s]
2 of 3 FAIL 3 accepted_values_stg_orders_status__completed__pending__cancelled [FAIL 3 in 0.7s]
3 of 3 SKIP relation analytics.fct_daily_revenue ............ [SKIP]

Finished running 1 view model, 1 test, 1 skipped in 2.10s.
Completed with 1 error and 0 warnings

Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=1 TOTAL=3

# Process exit code: 1  (CI fails the pipeline)
codeExamples.commonIssues: Interpreting SKIP as a bug in fct_daily_revenue - it is intentional because its upstream test failed; fix the data/logic in stg_orders. Expecting exit code 0 - a failing test returns exit code 1 so CI correctly fails.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Set test severity (warn vs error) deliberately: use warn for advisory checks so they surface as WARN without SKIPping downstreams, and error for critical checks that must halt the build.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce company runs a nightly dbt job on Snowflake to build its reporting layer. Occasionally upstream raw data has bad values, and with the old 'dbt run then dbt test' approach, corrupt numbers reached the finance dashboard before tests caught them. The team wants a fail-fast, CI-gated build that stops bad data mid-pipeline and rebuilds only what changed.
endToEndExample.inputData: Raw tables loaded hourly by Fivetran: raw.orders (id, customer_id, status, amount_cents, created_at) and raw.customers. Occasionally 'status' contains an unexpected value and 'amount_cents' has nulls. A prior production run's manifest.json is stored as a CI artifact.
endToEndExample.architecture: Fivetran does Extract+Load into Snowflake. A dbt project has staging views (stg_orders, stg_customers) and a mart table (fct_daily_revenue) plus generic tests. Airflow triggers 'dbt build' nightly against target=prod; a CI pipeline runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' on pull requests using the stored manifest.
processingSteps: 1. On a PR, CI runs 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts', so only changed models and their downstreams build, deferring unchanged upstreams to the prod objects.
2. dbt parses the project, computes the DAG, and applies the selector to pick just the modified subgraph.
3. It builds stg_orders (view), then immediately runs its not_null and accepted_values tests as zero-row SELECTs.
4. If a test fails (ERROR), dbt marks the downstream fct_daily_revenue as SKIP and returns exit code 1, failing the CI check so the bad change cannot merge.

5. On the nightly prod run, 'dbt build --target prod --threads 8' rebuilds the full DAG fail-fast; on success it writes run_results.json and returns exit code 0, and Airflow marks the task successful.
endToEndExample.output: A validated Snowflake table analytics.fct_daily_revenue rebuilt nightly, with a machine-readable run_results.json recording each model and test's status and timing. In CI, a pass/fail signal gates every merge.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Airflow tracks task success/failure via dbt's exit code; run_results.json is ingested to chart per-model timing and PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP counts; source freshness checks warn if Fivetran data is stale; Snowflake query history tracks compute per run.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Because the job uses dbt build, a failing test ERRORs the offending node and SKIPs its downstream dependents so bad revenue never reaches the dashboard; the non-zero exit code fails the orchestrator task, an alert fires, and the run is safely re-run after the data issue is fixed (materializations are idempotent).
endToEndExample.finalResult: Bad data is now stopped mid-DAG instead of surfacing on a finance slide; CI builds only changed nodes so it is fast and cheap; and every nightly run is observable via artifacts and gated by exit codes, giving finance a trustworthy daily-revenue table.

industryUseCases.problem: Nightly reporting builds occasionally shipped corrupt finance numbers because tests ran only after every model was already built.
industryUseCases.solution: Switch scheduled jobs to 'dbt build' so each model's tests run immediately and failures SKIP downstream marts, halting bad data mid-DAG.
industryUseCases.benefits: Finance-trusted daily tables, no bad numbers reaching dashboards, and clear ERROR/SKIP diagnostics pinpointing the failing upstream node.

industryUseCases.company: High-growth B2B SaaS with large dbt projects
industryUseCases.problem: As the project grew to hundreds of models, running the whole project on every pull request became slow and expensive.
industryUseCases.solution: Adopt slim CI with 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' against a stored production manifest to build only changed nodes and their children.
industryUseCases.benefits: CI run time and warehouse compute dropped sharply while still testing everything affected by a change, speeding up merges.

industryUseCases.company: Data platform teams running dbt in orchestrators (Airflow/Dagster)
industryUseCases.problem: They needed reliable pass/fail signals and per-model observability to trigger alerts and retries automatically.
industryUseCases.solution: Rely on dbt's process exit codes to fail orchestrator tasks and ingest run_results.json/manifest.json for per-node timing, status, and lineage.
industryUseCases.benefits: Automated alerting on failures, idempotent safe retries, and dashboards of model timings and test-failure trends across runs.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Scale by raising --threads so independent DAG branches run in parallel and by sizing the warehouse to the workload; use state:modified+ to build only changed nodes in CI and incremental materializations so large tables process only new rows instead of full-rebuilding each run.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: dbt build stops failures from propagating by marking dependents SKIP; runs are idempotent (models rebuild from their SELECTs, incrementals MERGE on a unique key) so retries are safe, and --fail-fast can abort early to conserve compute when any node errors.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: dbt is a stateless build step - it can rerun anywhere with the same repo, artifacts, and credentials; availability rests on the managed cloud warehouse and the orchestrator, and any run can be reproduced from git plus stored artifacts.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Since models are code and raw sources are immutable, the entire transformed layer can be rebuilt from scratch with 'dbt build --full-refresh' against retained raw data; stored manifest/run_results artifacts let you reconstruct exactly what a prior run did.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Increase threads for parallelism, tune warehouse SQL (filter early, avoid needless table materializations), use --defer with a prod manifest so unchanged upstreams are not rebuilt in CI, and reserve --full-refresh for logic/schema changes rather than every run.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Avoid blanket --full-refresh, prefer incremental materializations for big append-heavy tables, select only modified nodes (state:modified+) in CI, and schedule builds to real freshness needs so the warehouse recomputes only what is necessary.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Select environments with --target so prod runs use a least-privilege service role scoped to managed schemas; keep credentials in profiles.yml/secrets rather than code, and never run production builds under a personal or admin account.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Ingest run_results.json (per-node status, timing, SQL) and manifest.json (graph/lineage) into monitoring; track PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP counts, model durations, and test-failure trends, and alert on any non-zero exit code from a run/build.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use dbt build so generic tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships) and singular tests run interleaved with model builds; set critical checks to error severity so failures ERROR and SKIP dependents, and advisory checks to warn so they surface without halting the DAG.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: dbt logs each node and test result to stdout and to run_results.json; wire the orchestrator to alert on failed builds (non-zero exit code) and on test ERRORs/WARNs, and surface source-freshness warnings so stale upstream data is caught before builds run on it.

recommendedPractices: **Use dbt build for scheduled and CI runs** so models and their tests run together fail-fast and failures SKIP downstream nodes.
**Select only what changed** with state:modified+ (and --defer) in CI instead of rebuilding the entire project on every pull request.
**Treat exit codes as the source of truth** in orchestration - fail the task on any non-zero code and alert on it.
**Reserve --full-refresh for logic or schema changes** on incremental models rather than applying it to every run.
engineeringStandards: Run 'dbt build' in CI on pull requests so no change merges without models and tests passing together.
Store and version run artifacts (manifest.json, run_results.json) so state-based selection and monitoring work reliably.
Use --target to separate dev and prod, and run production builds under a scoped service role, never a personal account.
designRecommendations: Design incremental models with a proper unique_key so reruns MERGE idempotently and never duplicate rows.
Keep the DAG well-layered (staging -> intermediate -> marts) so selectors like model+ target coherent subgraphs.
Set test severity intentionally (error for critical, warn for advisory) so build halts only on the failures that truly must stop the pipeline.
namingConventions: Tag models by domain (tag:finance, tag:daily) so you can select and schedule cohesive groups with --select tag:.
Name models by layer and grain (stg_orders, fct_daily_revenue) so downstream selectors and logs read clearly.
Name CI jobs/targets explicitly (ci, prod, dev) so --target usage is unambiguous across environments.
documentationStandards: Document which command each scheduled job runs (build vs run vs test) and its selection flags so on-call engineers understand scope.
Record the meaning of each test and its severity so a FAIL/WARN in the summary is immediately actionable.
Document the slim-CI setup (state:modified+, --defer, --state path) so the artifact-comparison flow is reproducible.
testingStrategies: Add generic tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values, relationships) to keys and critical columns so build validates them per node.
Run source freshness checks before builds so stale raw data is caught before models build on it.
Gate merges with 'dbt build --select state:modified+' in CI so failing data quality blocks the change from reaching production.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming 'dbt run' also runs tests, and treating a green run as validated data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The word 'run' sounds all-encompassing, and beginners do not realize run and test are separate verbs.
commonMistakes.impact: Untested data is materialized and consumed downstream; data-quality issues go undetected until they surface in dashboards.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use dbt test to validate, or better, use dbt build in production so each model's tests run right after it builds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using separate 'dbt run then dbt test' in production instead of dbt build.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the legacy two-step workflow from early dbt and lingers in old pipelines and tutorials.
commonMistakes.impact: Every model builds first, so bad data propagates into all downstream tables before any test runs, wasting compute and reaching consumers.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Run dbt build so tests interleave with builds and a failing test SKIPs downstream dependents, stopping bad data mid-DAG.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting --full-refresh after changing an incremental model's logic or schema.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Incremental runs succeed silently by appending/merging, so nothing signals that historical rows are now inconsistent.
commonMistakes.impact: The table contains a mix of old and new logic, producing subtly wrong results that are hard to trace back to the change.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Run 'dbt run --select the_model --full-refresh' (or build) after changing incremental logic to drop and rebuild the table from scratch.

comparisonSection.explanation: dbt build traverses one combined DAG, building each model and immediately running its tests (plus seeds and snapshots), and marks downstream nodes SKIP when an upstream node errors or a test fails - so bad data is stopped mid-pipeline. Running 'dbt run' then 'dbt test' builds every model first and only tests afterward, meaning bad data has already propagated into all downstream tables before any test runs, and it ignores seeds/snapshots. build is the recommended production command precisely because it fails fast.

Running the whole project rebuilds and tests everything, which is simple but slow and expensive as projects grow, and wastes compute re-running unchanged models. Node selection with graph operators and state comparison builds only the nodes you target - typically what changed plus its descendants - making CI and scheduled runs fast and cheap while still validating everything affected. The trade-off is added selector complexity, but for anything beyond a tiny project, selective builds are the standard.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between dbt run and dbt test?
beginnerQuestions.answer: dbt run builds only your models - it compiles them and issues the materialization SQL (CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT) in DAG order, but it does not run any tests. dbt test runs only your data tests, compiling each into a SELECT that should return zero failing rows and executing it against already-built models. Neither one does the other's job.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The key point is that they are separate: a successful dbt run does not mean your data passed any test. Mentioning that build combines them shows deeper understanding.

beginnerQuestions.question: Why is dbt build recommended over running models and tests separately?
beginnerQuestions.answer: dbt build runs models, tests, seeds, and snapshots in one DAG traversal and tests each node right after it builds, so if a test fails, dbt SKIPs the downstream models that depend on it. This stops bad data from propagating mid-run. Running dbt run then dbt test builds everything first, so bad data has already flowed into downstream tables before any test executes.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize 'fail-fast' and that SKIP prevents building on known-bad data. That interleaving is the whole reason build exists.

intermediateQuestions.question: What do PASS, WARN, ERROR, and SKIP mean in the dbt summary, and what does SKIP indicate?
intermediateQuestions.answer: PASS means the node (model or test) succeeded. WARN means a test failed but at 'warn' severity, so it is advisory and does not stop the run. ERROR means a model failed to build or a test failed at 'error' severity. SKIP means dbt did not execute the node because something it depends on ERRORed or FAILed. So SKIP is not a bug in the skipped model - the problem is upstream.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to see that you know SKIP is intentional protection, not a failure of the skipped node, and that severity controls WARN vs ERROR.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you rebuild only the models affected by a change, and what flag rebuilds an incremental model from scratch?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use node selection: 'dbt build --select my_model+' builds a model and everything downstream; in CI, 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state <prod_manifest>' builds only changed nodes and their children by comparing to a stored manifest. To rebuild an incremental model fully, add --full-refresh, which drops and recreates the table instead of merging only new rows.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show you know the + operators (downstream vs upstream), state:modified+ for slim CI, and that --full-refresh is needed after incremental logic/schema changes.

advancedQuestions.question: How does dbt integrate with CI/CD, using exit codes and run artifacts?
advancedQuestions.answer: Every dbt command returns a process exit code - 0 on success, 1 when there are errors (including failed tests), and 2 on usage/config errors - which CI uses to pass or fail the pipeline. dbt also writes run artifacts to target/: run_results.json (per-node status, timing, and SQL) and manifest.json (the project graph). CI compares the current manifest to a stored production manifest to drive state:modified+ selection and --defer, and ingests run_results.json for monitoring.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tie exit codes to gating merges and artifacts to both slim CI and observability. This shows you can operationalize dbt, not just run it locally.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain idempotency in dbt and why it makes reruns safe.
advancedQuestions.answer: dbt commands are idempotent: rerunning a model produces the same result rather than duplicating data. Table and view models use CREATE OR REPLACE (or drop-and-recreate), so a rerun rebuilds the object from its SELECT. Incremental models MERGE on a unique_key, so reruns update or insert without double-counting. This means when a scheduled job fails and is retried, you can safely rerun the failed nodes without corrupting data.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Call out the incremental unique_key as the crucial detail - without it, reruns can duplicate rows, breaking idempotency.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your nightly 'dbt run' followed by 'dbt test' occasionally lets a bad status value reach the finance dashboard because tests only run after everything is built. How do you redesign the job so bad data is stopped before it propagates, and how do you keep CI fast on a large project?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The root cause is ordering: run-then-test builds all models before testing, so bad data is already downstream. Switching to dbt build interleaves each model's tests and SKIPs dependents on failure. For CI speed, avoid rebuilding the whole project by selecting only changed nodes via state comparison and deferring unchanged upstreams.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Change the scheduled job to 'dbt build --target prod' so each model's tests run right after it builds and a failing test SKIPs downstream marts, keeping bad data out. Add error-severity tests (accepted_values, not_null) on the critical columns. For CI, run 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts' so only changed nodes and their children build, comparing against the stored prod manifest. Gate merges on the exit code and alert on non-zero results.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design how a growing analytics team should run dbt in both CI (on pull requests) and production (scheduled), ensuring data quality, fast feedback, and controlled cost.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use dbt build everywhere so models and tests run together fail-fast. In CI, run 'dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer' against a stored production manifest so only changed nodes and dependents build. In production, an orchestrator triggers 'dbt build --target prod --threads N' on schedule, fails the task on non-zero exit code, and ingests run_results.json for monitoring. Use incremental materializations for large tables and --full-refresh only on logic/schema changes.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: build's interleaved testing adds a little run time versus a raw run but buys fail-fast protection. state:modified+ and --defer add selector/artifact complexity but drastically cut CI cost and time. More threads speed runs but raise concurrent warehouse load and cost.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Raise --threads and warehouse size for parallelism, convert heavy tables to incremental, keep selective builds (state:modified+) in CI, partition the project into tagged domains for targeted scheduling, and store artifacts so state comparison and monitoring scale with the project.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: dbt run builds models only, dbt test runs data tests only, and dbt build runs models + tests + seeds + snapshots in one fail-fast DAG pass that SKIPs downstream nodes when an upstream node fails.
keyConcepts: dbt run = materialize models (CREATE TABLE/VIEW AS SELECT); no tests.
dbt test = run data tests (SELECTs expected to return 0 failing rows) on built models.
dbt build = models + tests + seeds + snapshots in DAG order, testing each node right after it builds.
SKIP means dbt did not run a node because an upstream node ERRORed or a test FAILed - the fix is upstream.
Node selection (--select/--exclude, model+, +model, tag:, state:modified+) controls exactly what runs; artifacts and exit codes drive CI.
commands: dbt run                                   # build models only (no tests)
dbt test                                  # run data tests on built models
dbt build                                 # models + tests + seeds + snapshots (recommended)
dbt run --select fct_events --full-refresh --threads 8 --target prod   # full rebuild of an incremental model
interviewPoints: run builds models, test runs tests, build interleaves both (plus seeds/snapshots) fail-fast.
build SKIPs downstream nodes on failure so bad data does not propagate; SKIP is intentional.
Summary line: PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP; WARN vs ERROR is set by test severity.
Node selection: model+ (downstream), +model (upstream), tag:, state:modified+ for slim CI.
Exit codes (0/1/2) gate CI; run_results.json and manifest.json enable monitoring and state selection.
quickNotes: --full-refresh drops and rebuilds incremental models from scratch (needed after logic/schema changes).
--threads sets parallelism across independent DAG branches; --target picks dev/prod profile.
dbt compile generates SQL without executing it; dbt seed loads CSVs; dbt snapshot captures SCD history.
Commands are idempotent: table/view models rebuild from SELECT, incrementals MERGE on unique_key - reruns are safe.
Artifacts (run_results.json, manifest.json) are written to target/ after every run/build.

keyTakeaways: dbt run builds only models, dbt test runs only data tests against already-built models, and dbt build combines models, tests, seeds, and snapshots into one DAG-ordered command - knowing which verb does what is fundamental.

dbt build is the recommended production command because it interleaves each model's tests right after it builds and SKIPs downstream dependents on failure, stopping bad data mid-DAG, unlike separate run-then-test which builds everything before testing.
The summary line PASS/WARN/ERROR/SKIP tells you what happened at a glance; SKIP is intentional protection meaning an upstream node failed, so the fix is always upstream, not in the skipped node.

Node selection (--select/--exclude with operators like model+, +model, tag:, and state:modified+ with --defer) plus --full-refresh, --threads, and --target let you build exactly the right subset fast, cheaply, and idempotently.

Run artifacts (run_results.json, manifest.json) written to target/ and process exit codes (0/1/2) make dbt runs observable and CI-friendly, gating merges and driving monitoring and slim-CI state comparison.
